The question this page answers

How are borrower reach, savers/depositors, nominal portfolio and provider structure changing in microfinance?

Banks and microfinance: borrower, saver and balance figures measure different things

Report an error

Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified primary tables record 93,118 active microfinance borrowers at end-2015 and 88,445 at end-2020; a 2024 policy paper citing SFD/SMED data reports 78,686 for end-2023, for a set of providers that has not yet been verified. Saver, portfolio and bank balance-sheet figures use different definitions, provider coverage and valuation bases, so this resource keeps them separate and does not read them as one trend or as deeper inclusion.

Explore questionsOpen evidence
What this does not establish

What the finance evidence does not establish

Savers or depositors are not necessarily unique people. Nominal portfolio growth is not real credit deepening. A listed microfinance bank is not proof of operation or outreach. A restatement of the same year's figures is not an economic boom. Historical or secondary borrower figures are not a current national inclusion rate, and these separate data points do not establish improved borrower outcomes or causality.

What we still do not know

What remains unresolved

This resource still lacks a fully harmonized current institution-level series that reconciles provider coverage, borrower and saver definitions, deduplication, currency and valuation basis, nominal versus real values, and comparable reporting periods. The underlying 2023 SFD/SMED primary source behind several secondary figures has been identified but is not yet available for direct verification. Microfinance portfolio figures are also not expressed here as a share of bank credit: twelve microfinance banks appear on the same bank list of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), so the two stocks may overlap, and they differ in valuation basis, date and institutional coverage.

03Analysis

Microfinance history is informative, but not a continuous annual series

The historical record contains exact quarterly and year-end observations, years for which only references are available, and years with no usable observation. In 2015, primary SFD evidence shows active borrowers declining from 124,917 at end-March to 106,825 at end-September and 93,118 at end-December, alongside a declining reported portfolio. This resource keeps those observed points and gaps as they are; it does not interpolate the missing months or estimate a causal conflict effect. Its starting point is dated in two ways: 1997, when the Social Fund for Development (SFD) was established, and 1998, when SFD began operations and became active in microfinance. The SFD terms of reference that date the start of microfinance to 1997 could not be re-opened (on 4 October 2026, and again on 10 October 2026), so that dating has not been re-read in the original for this edition.

04Analysis

Borrowers, savers and nominal portfolio do not form one harmonized trend

Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified primary tables record 93,118 active borrowers at end-2015 and 88,445 at end-2020. A 2024 policy paper citing SFD/SMED data reports 78,686 for end-2023; the set of providers it covers has not yet been verified. That paper also reports what it calls 3.3 million “active savers” and a nominal portfolio of about YER 44 billion in 2023. The verified 2020 figures are 1,611,206 savers/depositors and YER 33.379 billion; “active savers” and “savers/depositors” have not been shown to be the same measure. Both portfolio figures are nominal rials. Between December 2020 and December 2023 the average market rate published by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) moved from about 793 to about 1,529 rials per US dollar, and the evidence base does not record which rial valuation, across Yemen's divided monetary areas, the portfolio figures use. No real or US-dollar change can be derived from the two figures. With the 2023 primary source document, provider coverage, saver definition and the link between the two periods also unresolved, these values are separate data points, not a trend.

Another view of the evidence
05Analysis

Who provides microfinance: what the lists and panels show

Of the 26 banks on the list of licensed banks issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 3 October 2026, this resource describes 12 as microfinance banks on the basis of their names in the list; that description is not an independent regulatory classification, and appearing on the list establishes listing, not operation or outreach. Historical microfinance figures come from provider reporting panels whose membership changes — the 2014 panel, for example, covers nine providers — so provider counts and totals from different periods are not one continuous series.

06Evidence

A published balance-sheet jump can partly be a valuation change

The same 2022 consolidated banking positions are published at materially higher levels from the 2023 annual report onward, alongside a documented January-2023 shift to market-exchange-rate valuation of foreign-currency positions. The published difference does not by itself establish growth in assets, deposits or credit because the restatement changes the comparison base.

07System context

Finance sits between funding, providers and real economic use

Institutional finance connects funding and liquidity to providers, credit products, firms and households. But each link has a different measure: capital available to an institution is not credit disbursed; portfolio is not borrowers; borrowers are not unique households; and larger loans are not necessarily wider outreach. This resource links Finance to Firms, Providers and external flows while preserving those boundaries.

Another view of the evidence (2)

More evidence and context

More detail on this question, each item with its own period and limits.
System context

Balance-sheet capacity is visible; a complete current financial-soundness diagnosis is not

The compiled monetary series provide balance-sheet context on bank deposits, credit to the private sector, bank reserves, capital and reserves, loans and advances, and foreign-currency deposits across their available reporting periods. These measures help describe intermediation capacity and structure, but they are not a complete current financial-soundness assessment: solvency, asset quality or current system-wide soundness cannot be inferred from balance-sheet aggregates alone. The IMF's 2025 Article IV staff report does publish one set of financial soundness indicators for Yemen, sourced to the Yemeni authorities and IMF staff calculations, including the ratio of non-performing loans to total gross loans at each year-end from 2014 to 2024 and at one date in 2025. For each year-end from 2014 to 2019 that ratio is printed as zero, which this resource reads as not reported, not as zero. The table does not state which banks or areas it covers; the report says that the central bank began reporting a set of these indicators in 2025 and that comprehensive data are still being compiled, and its own text gives values for two other ratios that differ from the table. One published vintage of unstated coverage is not yet a harmonized series with common definitions, so this resource does not present these ratios as a series.

Analysis

External support passes through stages and forms that cannot simply be added together

A pledge, commitment, signed agreement, deposit, amount made available, budget disbursement, FX-auction use, in-kind support and project cost are different stages or forms of support. They may describe the same support pathway at different stages or overlapping components. This resource therefore does not manufacture a cumulative finance total by adding unlike amounts.

System context

The financial system changed through shocks, constraints and policy responses — not one continuous trend

The documented chronology traces several distinct breaks: reserve and import-finance pressure by 2015–16; the 2016 central-bank split; rapid growth of currency outside banks by 2017; Saudi reserve support in 2018 and 2023; the 2019 split in cash circulation and payments; the oil-export shock after 2022; FX auctions and external support in 2023–24; banking-liquidity stress and administrative FX/import measures in 2025; and later payment-infrastructure investment. Each event keeps its territorial and institutional scope; where money is involved, agreement, deposit, availability, disbursement and downstream use are kept apart and never added together; and revisions to remittance figures for the same year are kept separate from actual economic change. These events help explain the environment in which finance operates, but their sequence does not prove that any one event caused a financial-inclusion outcome.

System context

An evidence-based chronology of the financial system

The dated events below help explain the conditions under which finance operates: funding and liquidity pressures, exchange-rate conditions, intermediation and payment infrastructure. Each event opens a record with its source and limitations. The chronology is context, not a causal model of financial inclusion.

Demand-side evidence

Holding a product and owning an account are related — not interchangeable

Product-holding and mobile-access figures attributed to the OECD's 2026 financial-sector review have not yet been verified against the review's own text, and they are not shown here. Any such measures would in any case use questions and constructs different from the Global Findex account-ownership measure and would remain separate evidence rather than a harmonised series. Product holding, account ownership, device access and financial-service use must not be averaged or treated as interchangeable.

Dated events in Yemen's financial system

Each event keeps its date, its source and what it does not establish. The order of events does not show that one caused another.

List of dated events (24)
  1. When was it measured or observed?2014–2015
    The conflict that escalated from late 2014 disrupted output, public finance, external inflows and monetary conditions; by late 2015 official foreign reserves had fallen below US$2 billion, about two months of imports.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: This conditions banks, import finance, cash demand and service continuity.
    Does not establish: It does not quantify population financial inclusion in 2015 or attribute later inclusion outcomes to one shock.
    Sources: Yemen's Economic Outlook, Spring 2016 · Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)
  2. When was it measured or observed?February 2016
    With reserves under pressure, the Central Bank of Yemen stopped supporting imports at the official exchange rate except for wheat and rice.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: Import-finance constraints affect liquidity, prices, firms and trade-settlement channels, but are not themselves an inclusion measure.
    Does not establish: It does not show which households or firms lost financial-service access.
    Sources: Yemen's Economic Outlook, Spring 2016
  3. When was it measured or observed?2016
    A 2016 decision relocated the Central Bank of Yemen from Sana'a to Aden, leaving two central-bank authorities operating under the divided political and territorial order.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: Provider status, payment interoperability, cash conditions and formal financial access can diverge by territory.
    Does not establish: Institutional fragmentation does not by itself prove that a specific provider or service stopped operating in a specific location.
    Sources: Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP, P180708): appraisal document (project approved 17 June 2025)
  4. When was it measured or observed?2017–2018
    World Bank monitoring estimated that currency outside banks rose from about YER 811 billion in 2014 to YER 1,673 billion by end-2017, alongside large issuance of new banknotes, and expected rapid money-supply growth in 2018.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: It provides context for cash dependence and pressure on formal intermediation.
    Does not establish: Currency outside banks is not equal to household cash holdings, exclusion, or the number of unbanked people.
    Sources: Yemen Economic Monitoring Brief, Fall 2018
  5. When was it measured or observed?March 2018
    Saudi Arabia issued a directive for, and then signed an agreement to deliver, a US$2 billion deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen, with the stated aim of supporting the financial and economic position and the riyal.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: Stabilization and import-finance support can affect firms, prices and banking liquidity indirectly.
    Does not establish: The signed amount is not identical to later FX sales and is not an inclusion outcome.
    Sources: Saudi directive and agreement on a US$2 billion deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen (January–March 2018)
  6. When was it measured or observed?December 2019
    Tighter enforcement in Sana'a of the ban on newer rial banknotes contributed to a payments crisis and widened dual exchange rates between old and new notes across the divided monetary areas.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: A nominally available transfer or payment channel may have different usability and cost by territory.
    Does not establish: It does not quantify unique users switching to digital finance or prove durable digital adoption.
    Sources: Yemen Monthly Economic Update, December 2019
  7. When was it measured or observed?Early 2020
    World Bank monitoring reported that the bulk of the 2018 Saudi US$2 billion deposit had been exhausted by end-January 2020 and highlighted multiple exchange-rate regimes and remittance risks from the COVID-19 shock.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: Remittances matter as both household flows and part of broader FX/payment conditions.
    Does not establish: A stated risk to remittances is not an observed decline unless separately measured.
    Sources: Yemen's Economic Update, April 2020 · Saudi directive and agreement on a US$2 billion deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen (January–March 2018)
  8. When was it measured or observed?October 2022–January 2023
    Attacks on oil export facilities in October 2022 were followed by the suspension of oil exports from January 2023, sharply reducing a major source of government and foreign-exchange revenue in areas under the internationally recognized government.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: Bank liquidity, FX availability, firm finance and payment conditions need to be read against this external-revenue break.
    Does not establish: The oil-export shock does not itself quantify access to financial services or household adoption.
    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)
  9. When was it measured or observed?21 February 2023
    Saudi Arabia signed a US$1 billion deposit agreement with the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) and stated that the amount was fully deposited in the bank's account.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: The link to inclusion is indirect through macro stability, banking and import-finance conditions.
    Does not establish: The US$0.775 billion later made available and any use of it in FX auctions are part of the same US$1 billion, not additional support.
    Sources: Agreement on a US$1 billion Saudi deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen (21 February 2023)
  10. When was it measured or observed?2023–2024
    The IMF reports US$1.2 billion in Saudi budget support over 2023–24 and a US$1 billion deposit at the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), of which US$0.775 billion had been made available; CBY-Aden auctioned US$1.05 billion for import financing during 2023–24.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: These flows condition formal banking and firm activity but are not direct inclusion outcomes.
    Does not establish: The US$1.05 billion of FX auctions is downstream use of support already counted, not a separate donor inflow.
    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80) · Agreement on a US$1 billion Saudi deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen (21 February 2023)
  11. When was it measured or observed?2022–2024
    In the IMF’s macroeconomic framework for areas under the internationally recognized government, the current-account deficit improved from about 40.5% of GDP in 2022 to an average of about 14.5% in 2023–24, reflecting import compression, strong remittances and bilateral grants despite the halt in oil exports.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: Remittances, imports and FX conditions interact, but the aggregate balance does not reveal who used formal services.
    Does not establish: The deficit improvement is not proof of stronger household welfare, financial inclusion or productive investment.
    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)
  12. When was it measured or observed?March–June 2024
    A new 100-rial coin in Sana'a in March 2024 was followed by an April CBY-Aden directive for banks headquartered in Sana'a to relocate to Aden and further June measures affecting unlicensed entities, wallets, payment services and remittance networks.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: The same provider name can carry different regulatory and operational meanings by territory.
    Does not establish: A directive or prohibition does not prove actual compliance, closure, relocation or user access at every location.
    Sources: Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP, P180708): appraisal document (project approved 17 June 2025) · Circular prohibiting dealings with unlicensed electronic wallets and payment services (26 June 2024) · Governor's Decision No. 23 of 2024 on domestic money-transfer activity (26 June 2024; ref. 343/CBY/2024)
  13. When was it measured or observed?By 30 May 2024
    World Bank/G2Px reported that Yemen's Unconditional Cash Transfer programme had piloted digital payments in eight districts, reaching 45,460 recipients, with the pilot emphasizing payments into fully functional accounts and recipient choice.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: This is direct Yemen evidence that a social transfer can create formal account exposure. Durable inclusion still requires follow-up on activation, repeat transactions, merchant use, saving, cash-out, cost and user experience.
    Does not establish: The 45,460 recipients are not evidence of 45,460 persistent active users, a national inclusion rate, or sustained post-transfer digital use.
    Sources: Digitalizing Government-to-Person (G2P) Payments in Yemen: unconditional cash transfer (UCT) pilot (2024)
  14. When was it measured or observed?2024 value as revised between CBY-Aden annual reports
    The 2024 annual report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) gives remittances for 2024 of USD 6,245 million; its 2025 annual report restates the same year at USD 3,422.16 million, a downward revision of about 45.2%.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: Any analysis of remittance trends must disclose changes between report editions and in method before drawing behavioural conclusions.
    Does not establish: A revised 2024 level is not evidence that remittances collapsed by 45.2% during 2024.
    Sources: Annual Report 2024 · Annual Report 2025
  15. When was it measured or observed?2022–April 2025
    According to the IMF staff report, which focuses on areas under the internationally recognized government, the banking sector's ratio of liquid assets to short-term liabilities fell from 148 in 2022 to 69 in April 2025, while its capital-to-assets ratio fell from about 5 in 2022 to 2.5 in April 2025.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: Provider resilience and usable service capacity are system conditions for inclusion.
    Does not establish: Prudential ratios do not show how many unique people gained or lost access.
    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)
    These values are from the text of the staff report (paragraph 13). The report's own table of financial soundness indicators (Table 5) gives different values and dates for the same two ratios. Neither the text nor the table states a unit. The report says its data relate to areas under the authorities' control unless otherwise stated (paragraph 2), but its statistical annex says the banks' balance-sheet data cover the whole of Yemen (Annex IV); it does not state the coverage of these two ratios.
  16. When was it measured or observed?17 June 2025–2030 project period
    The World Bank approved a US$20 million IDA grant for the Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (P180708) on 17 June 2025. The project is active, implemented by UNDP, closes on 30 June 2030, and the latest publicly disclosed Implementation Status and Results Report (ISR) identified for this resource is report no. 2, dated 8 April 2026.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: The project can create payment-system capacity and targeted access/usage mechanisms, while population adoption and inclusion effects require later evidence.
    Does not establish: The US$20 million commitment, an implementation report, a system go-live or a 2030 target is not evidence that users have already adopted services or that inclusion outcomes have been achieved.
    Sources: Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP, P180708): project record and results framework (2025–2030) · Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP): implementation overview (2025–2030) · Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP): Implementation Status and Results Report, sequence 2 (8 April 2026)
  17. When was it measured or observed?July 2025 onward
    The internationally recognized government established the National Committee for the Regulation and Financing of Imports to prioritize FX use for essential imports, enhance import transparency and channel FX into the formal banking sector.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: This may change incentives and flows through banks and exchangers, which should be measured.
    Does not establish: Creation of the committee does not prove improved access, lower costs or successful formalization.
    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)
  18. When was it measured or observed?Mid-July–early August 2025
    The IMF reports the rial, in markets in areas under the internationally recognized government, strengthening from about YER2,900 to about YER1,600 per US dollar from mid-July to early August 2025 after a package of FX and market measures.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: Exchange-rate conditions affect prices, remittance conversion, firm costs and channel incentives.
    Does not establish: The appreciation does not by itself prove durable macro stability or improved financial inclusion.
    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)
  19. When was it measured or observed?September 2025
    The IMF reports operational foreign-exchange reserves of US$350 million in September 2025, covering about one month of imports.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: Reserve scarcity affects import finance, bank liquidity and prices.
    Does not establish: Import-cover reserves do not measure household financial resilience or account use.
    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)
    This value and its date are from the text of the staff report (paragraph 12). The debt sustainability analysis published in the same country report gives reserves of the same amount as of June 2025.
  20. When was it measured or observed?1 March 2026
    The Saudi Development and Reconstruction Program for Yemen signed an agreement with Yemen's Ministry of Finance to begin depositing SAR1.3 billion in economic support for operating expenses and salaries.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: It can affect public cash flow, salaries, demand and macro conditions.
    Does not establish: The SAR1.3 billion agreement is not shown to be the same flow as IMF-reported USD commitments or disbursements; no source-level crosswalk establishes that. An agreement to deposit is not evidence that a deposit or a disbursement has taken place.
    Sources: Agreement between the Saudi Development and Reconstruction Program for Yemen (SDRPY) and Yemen's Ministry of Finance on SAR1.3 billion in economic support (1 March 2026)
  21. When was it measured or observed?4 June 2026
    The World Bank Group's Board of Executive Directors approved a Country Partnership Framework for Yemen for FY2026–FY2030 and approved four new operations totaling US$285 million. The framework focuses on nutrition, electricity, agribusiness, mariculture and fisheries, with women’s participation and private-sector development as cross-cutting enablers.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: This context helps interpret firm finance, payment infrastructure and participation constraints as connected parts of a wider economic system.
    Does not establish: Endorsement of a strategy or approval of operations does not prove improved financial access, service use, jobs, implementation quality or inclusion outcomes.
    Sources: Republic of Yemen: Country Partnership Framework for FY2026–FY2030
  22. When was it measured or observed?30 June 2026
    The World Bank approved a US$100 million IDA grant for the Cash for Nutrition and Livelihoods Project in Yemen. The project is expected to reach 1.8 million people, support around 55,000 individuals through Village Savings and Loan Associations, and support more than 675,000 people in obtaining national identity cards and birth certificates; these are design features and targets of the project, not achieved results.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: Identity documentation and savings-group participation are potentially important enabling steps that should be measured separately from account ownership, active use and service quality.
    Does not establish: Project targets, beneficiary counts, identity-document support and VSLA participation do not establish national prevalence, active bank or wallet use, or persistence after programme support ends.
    Sources: Cash for Nutrition and Livelihoods Project, Yemen (approved 30 June 2026)
  23. When was it measured or observed?16 July 2026
    IMF staff and the Yemeni authorities reached a staff-level agreement on policies that could underpin a proposed 18-month Staff-Monitored Program. The agreement is subject to IMF Management approval, and the IMF press release on the mission states that it will not result in an Executive Board discussion; priorities include fiscal and monetary management, reserve rebuilding, and financial-sector and electricity reforms.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: Financial-sector reform commitments matter for intermediation, resilience and oversight, while inclusion effects require later evidence on provider behaviour, access, use, cost, quality and protection.
    Does not establish: A staff-level agreement does not establish IMF financing, Executive Board approval, completed reforms, improved bank soundness or improved financial inclusion.
    Sources: Yemen: staff-level agreement on a proposed Staff-Monitored Program (16 July 2026)
  24. When was it measured or observed?Current analytical rule
    The chronology treats remittances, international support, FX auctions, import compression, reserve changes, bank liquidity, regulatory actions and payment infrastructure as related but non-interchangeable kinds of evidence.
    Relevance to financial inclusion: This is the bridge from macro-financial chronology to inclusion decisions: capacity, access, use, quality and outcomes remain separate states.
    Does not establish: Chronological proximity never substitutes for causal identification.

When the baseline moves
Yemen’s banking series shows why a large published jump must be separated from a change in measurement before it becomes an economic story.

What exactly do we mean by microfinance growth?
Yemen’s microfinance record does not move on one axis. Borrower counts, saver or depositor measures, nominal portfolios and institutional form are not the same measure, and they do not yet form one harmonised growth series.

What measurement would change the decision?

Measurement priorityP0 · Firms / MSME
A current MSME finance demand/use baseline
The 2022 Yemen Enterprise Survey (formal firms in seven governorates) and programme evidence from the Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) can each be used within its own scope; neither supplies a current representative national MSME finance baseline.
Evidence needed: A representative survey of firms/MSMEs, or validated administrative data linked to firm-level data, with explicit definitions, covering finance need, application, approval or rejection, amount, terms, source, use, repayment pressure and outcome.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show the finance journey from need and application through approval or rejection, terms, use and repayment pressure, while SMEPS remains a separate programme-evidence layer.
Open this measurement priority
Measurement priorityP1 · Credit infrastructure / MSME
Credit-infrastructure reach and actual use
Legal texts, project documents and institutional records can establish that credit infrastructure exists or is being developed; lender participation, inquiry use and borrower reach are not yet documented as one complete evidence chain.
Evidence needed: Administrative data from credit-information and collateral infrastructure and participating institutions on coverage, inquiries, report use, collateral registration, lender participation and borrower type.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show whether credit infrastructure enters actual lending decisions, for which lenders and borrower groups.

Informative history without a continuous annual series
The historical microfinance evidence is informative but does not form a continuous annual series. This resource keeps the exact quarterly and year-end points, anomalies, years known only through a reference in another source, and years with no data, rather than filling the gaps.
Who or what does it apply to? Source-specific microfinance observations whose provider/reporting universe can vary by point; each observation retains its own source and status.

Borrower, saver and portfolio figures come from different sources and definitions and do not yet form one trend
Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified primary tables record 93,118 active borrowers at end-2015 and 88,445 at end-2020. A 2024 policy paper citing SFD/SMED data reports 78,686 at end-2023; the set of providers it covers has not been verified. The same paper reports what it calls 3.3 million “active savers” at microfinance banks in 2023 and a nominal portfolio of about YER44 billion; the verified 2020 anchors are 1,611,206 savers/depositors and YER33.379 billion. “Active savers” and “savers/depositors” have not been shown to be the same measure, and both portfolio figures are nominal rials: between December 2020 and December 2023 the average market rate published by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) moved from about 793 to about 1,529 rials per US dollar, and the evidence base does not record which rial valuation, across Yemen's divided monetary areas, the portfolio figures use, so no real or US-dollar change can be derived from them. Because the 2023 primary source document, the exact set of providers covered, saver definition/deduplication and period bridge are not yet available in the evidence base for direct verification, these are separate reference points, each with stated limits, not a trend. Together they do not establish unique people, real credit growth, broader inclusion, improved borrower outcomes or causality.
Who or what does it apply to? Microfinance borrower, saver/depositor and nominal-portfolio measures drawn from provider and reporting groups defined by each source, which are not yet fully harmonized across years.

  • OECD, IMF Executive Board and Yemeni authorities: institutional fragility, weak formal access and correspondent banking (qualitative accounts)
  • 2015 Q4 microfinance observation with a portfolio contradiction
  • 1997 institutional origin and 1998 operational programme start
  • Microfinance in 2014 — two comparable quarters, not a long trend
  • 2015: a sharp fall in active borrowers within the year
  • Commercial and Islamic banks: consolidated assets at the end of May 2026
